description: Hi everyone! I am participating solo in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge for the Delhi Local Event. I'm working on the Space Mission Design Game challenge, designing an interactive game concept and rulebook where players make strategic engineering, resource, and budget trade-offs for space missions. Super excited to build, learn, and create!
summary:
Shackleton Station is a free, browser-based 3D game where you command a Moon base near the lunar south pole. You pack a lander within a budget and weight limit. Then you keep four astronauts alive for 30 days through the two-week lunar night, solar flares, moon dust, meteorites and radio blackouts.

It addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by turning real mission-design thinking into play. Players choose equipment, balance power, oxygen, water and food, and handle risks, so they feel real trade-offs like mass, cost and safety. Mission Control explains every rule and event by voice and visuals. Students learn without reading long text, and a daily quiz reinforces facts from NASA sources.

It matters because space missions are hard to picture, and most students never see the engineering behind them. Learning by playing makes the science memorable. It shows that surviving off Earth depends on planning, teamwork and science. The game runs in any modern browser with no login, so any classroom can use it. It can inspire the next generation of engineers, scientists and astronauts for the Artemis era.
details:
What does my project do and how does it work?
You are the mission controller of a Moon base.

  1. Mission Control (a voice with captions) explains the rules and every piece of equipment, with animations.
  2. You pack the lander. You have 1,000 credits and a 10 tonne limit for solar panels, batteries, a fission power unit, an ice-mining rig, a greenhouse, a rover, a radiation shelter, supplies and spare parts.
  3. You land in a 3D Moon base with four astronauts: Luna (geologist), Sirius (engineer), Altair (botanist) and Yuri (medic).
  4. Each day, every astronaut does one job: mine ice, grow food, collect samples, repair, rest or build.
  5. When you end the day, something happens: a solar flare, dust storm, meteorite, blackout, bonus cargo or funding cut. Mission Control explains it, shares a fact and asks a quiz question for bonus credits.
  6. Survive 30 days to win a rank (Cadet, Pilot, Commander or Legend). If the base runs out of power, oxygen, water or crew, you lose, and the game explains why.

What benefits does it have?

  • Students learn how a real mission works without reading long text.
  • It trains planning, trade-offs and problem solving.
  • It is free, needs no login or install, and works on a laptop or phone.
  • It has captions and sound options, and every rule is shown as well as spoken.

What is the intended impact?
To make high schoolers curious about space engineering and see that a Moon base is a puzzle of power, water, food, safety and teamwork. Teachers can use it as a 15 to 20 minute classroom activity. I hope it inspires some students to explore STEM careers.

What tool did I used?
Claude (by Anthropic) wrote all the code and made the presentation. The game also runs on the open-source Three.js 3D library, which loads in the page. If the form asks for tools, you may want to mention Three.js too. All graphics are drawn in code and all sounds are made in the browser.

How is my project creative?

  • A spoken, animated tour of the equipment, so players hear and see the rules.
  • Named astronauts with real roles and skills, whose names float over their heads in the 3D base.
  • Real Moon phenomena as game events, each explained in plain language.
  • A daily quiz for bonus credits, and a home page set in a mission control room on Earth.
  • Dramatic win and lose endings that show your score and what to do better.

What factors did I considered?
I worked solo and considered:

  • Audience: high schoolers, so low reading and friendly language.
  • Accessibility: captions, voice and sound toggles, mobile layout, and no login.
  • Science: the Moon’s day and night, ice at the south pole, radiation and dust.
  • Balance: the game is hard but fair, and I tested it with automated playthroughs.
  • Rules: I used no NASA logos, flags or images of people under 18.
